title: SuperEnalotto Game Overview and Current Matrix: Six from Ninety
description:
This Signature edition presents an original study of the same subject, written as Signature-original material. Where a point is a design proposal rather than a verified public fact, it is labeled as a Signature design in the text, and it is never presented as an authentic public record.

SuperEnalotto is Italy's national lottery, operated by Sisal. A player chooses six numbers from 1 to 90, and the draw selects six main numbers plus extra numbers described in later records. A single line costs 1 euro, a price that doubled from 0.50 euros on 2 February 2026 after more than a decade at the old price. The minimum jackpot is 2,000,000 euros, and there is no cap on how high the jackpot can grow.

The matrix is the whole story of the game's odds. Choosing six numbers from ninety gives 622,614,630 possible combinations, which is why SuperEnalotto has the longest jackpot odds of any major national lottery. The game was first drawn on 3 December 1997 as the successor to Italy's earlier Enalotto lottery, and it has been drawn ever since, with its schedule growing from three draws a week to four.

Lottery outcomes are random. No past result changes the odds of the next draw, and no frequency, hot, cold, or overdue analysis in this record improves the chance of a future result.

title: SuperEnalotto Exact Jackpot Odds by Combination Counting
description:
This Signature edition presents an original study of the same subject, written as Signature-original material. Where a point is a design proposal rather than a verified public fact, it is labeled as a Signature design in the text, and it is never presented as an authentic public record.

The jackpot odds are not an estimate or a rounded marketing figure; they are an exact count. The number of ways to choose six numbers from ninety is the binomial coefficient C(90,6), which equals 90 times 89 times 88 times 87 times 86 times 85 divided by 6 factorial. That arithmetic gives 622,614,630, and because exactly one of those combinations is drawn as the six main numbers, the chance for any one line is 1 in 622,614,630.

To put that number in scale: buying 100 different lines in one draw gives 100 chances out of 622,614,630, which is about 1 in 6,226,146. Buying every combination would cost 622,614,630 euros at 1 euro a line, far more than any jackpot except the very largest, and it would still share the jackpot with any other winner. The odds are the same for every combination, including birthdays, patterns, and consecutive numbers.

Lottery outcomes are random. No past result changes the odds of the next draw, and no frequency, hot, cold, or overdue analysis in this record improves the chance of a future result.

Labeling note: this Signature record is Signature-original. Verified public facts it repeats are the same facts as in the public edition; any framing, ordering, or extension beyond them is Signature design, not a public record.

import math
total = math.comb(90, 6)
print("C(90,6) =", total)
print("jackpot odds for one line: 1 in", total)
for lines in [1, 10, 100, 1000]:
    print(lines, "lines -> about 1 in", total // lines)
print("cost of every combination at 1 euro per line (euros):", total)

title: SuperEnalotto All Prize-Tier Odds
description:
This Signature edition presents an original study of the same subject, written as Signature-original material. Where a point is a design proposal rather than a verified public fact, it is labeled as a Signature design in the text, and it is never presented as an authentic public record.

SuperEnalotto pays at six main tiers. Matching all six main numbers wins the jackpot, at 1 in 622,614,630. Matching five main numbers plus the Jolly number wins the second tier, at 1 in 103,769,105. Matching five main numbers without the Jolly wins the third tier, at 1 in 1,250,230. Matching four wins at 1 in 11,907, matching three at 1 in 327, and matching two at 1 in 22. The published figures for the lower tiers are rounded from exact fractions, and the demo shows both the exact counts and the published rounded odds.

The exact counts come from the same combination logic as the jackpot. For the second tier there are 6 ways to choose which five of the six main numbers are matched, and the sixth chosen number must be the single Jolly number, giving 6 favourable combinations. For the third tier the sixth number can be any of the 83 numbers that are neither a main number nor the Jolly, giving 6 times 83, or 498, favourable combinations. The same counting gives the remaining tiers, and the demo verifies each tier against the published odds.

Adding the six tier chances gives the overall chance of any main-game prize, roughly 1 in 21 to 1 in 22 depending on rounding and on whether instant-win prizes are counted. That overall figure is dominated by the two-number tier and says nothing about the jackpot, which remains 1 in 622,614,630. Lottery outcomes are random. No past result changes the odds of the next draw, and no frequency, hot, cold, or overdue analysis in this record improves the chance of a future result.

Labeling note: this Signature record is Signature-original. Verified public facts it repeats are the same facts as in the public edition; any framing, ordering, or extension beyond them is Signature design, not a public record.

demo.code:
import math
total = math.comb(90, 6)
tiers = [("6", math.comb(6, 6) * math.comb(84, 0)),
         ("5+Jolly", math.comb(6, 5) * 1),
         ("5", math.comb(6, 5) * 83),
         ("4", math.comb(6, 4) * math.comb(84, 2)),
         ("3", math.comb(6, 3) * math.comb(84, 3)),
         ("2", math.comb(6, 2) * math.comb(84, 4))]
any_p = 0.0
for name, fav in tiers:
    p = fav / total
    any_p += p
    print(name, "favourable:", fav, "| odds about 1 in", round(total / fav))
print("overall chance of any main tier:", round(any_p, 5), "= about 1 in", round(1 / any_p))

title: SuperEnalotto Jolly Number Mechanics
description:
This Signature edition presents an original study of the same subject, written as Signature-original material. Where a point is a design proposal rather than a verified public fact, it is labeled as a Signature design in the text, and it is never presented as an authentic public record.

The Jolly is a seventh number drawn from the balls remaining after the six main numbers have been drawn. A player does not choose the Jolly; it is drawn from the 84 numbers that were not drawn as main numbers. The Jolly matters only to a player who has already matched five of the six main numbers: matching five mains plus the Jolly wins the second tier, while matching five mains without the Jolly wins the third tier.

The distinction matters because the second tier is much rarer than the third. There are only 6 combinations that match five mains plus the Jolly, against 498 that match five mains without it, so the second-tier odds are 1 in 103,769,105 while the third-tier odds are 1 in 1,250,230. A player who matches five mains has no control over whether the Jolly completes the set; the Jolly is simply the next ball drawn, and it either is the player's sixth number or it is not.

Historically the Jolly was taken from the Venice regional Lotto draw before 1 July 2009, when SuperEnalotto numbers were derived from regional draws. Since then all SuperEnalotto numbers, including the Jolly, have been drawn independently. Lottery outcomes are random. No past result changes the odds of the next draw, and no frequency, hot, cold, or overdue analysis in this record improves the chance of a future result.

title: SuperEnalotto SuperStar Option Mechanics
description:
This Signature edition presents an original study of the same subject, written as Signature-original material. Where a point is a design proposal rather than a verified public fact, it is labeled as a Signature design in the text, and it is never presented as an authentic public record.

SuperStar is an optional add-on costing 0.50 euros per line. The player picks a SuperStar number from 1 to 90, and a SuperStar number is drawn separately after the main numbers and the Jolly. Matching the SuperStar number multiplies main-game prizes, by up to 100 times according to the operator, and it also creates prizes for matching the SuperStar number with zero, one, or two main numbers, which would otherwise win nothing.

Two fixed additions are also attached to SuperStar. A jackpot won with SuperStar is 2,000,000 euros higher than the same jackpot without it, and a second-tier prize won with SuperStar is 1,000,000 euros higher. The SuperStar feature was introduced on 28 March 2006, and it increases the number of ways to win from six main tiers to fourteen combinations of main match and SuperStar match.

SuperStar does not change the odds of matching the six main numbers, which remain 1 in 622,614,630. It adds a separate 1-in-90 chance of matching the SuperStar number itself, and it changes what a win is worth, not how likely the main match is. Lottery outcomes are random. The schedule was Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday for most of the game's history, and an additional Friday draw was introduced in July 2023, so draws now normally take place four times a week: Tuesday, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday. title: SuperEnalotto Rollover Culture and No-Cap History
description:
This Signature edition presents an original study of the same subject, written as Signature-original material. Where a point is a design proposal rather than a verified public fact, it is labeled as a Signature design in the text, and it is never presented as an authentic public record.

SuperEnalotto has no jackpot cap and no rolldown: if nobody matches all six main numbers, the jackpot rolls over to the next draw and keeps growing until it is won. Combined with the 1-in-622,614,630 jackpot odds, that rule produces very long rollover runs and very large jackpots, and those runs are a genuine part of Italian lottery culture, with ticket sales rising as the jackpot grows and media coverage following each run.

The verified rollover runs illustrate the scale. The 2016 record of 163.5 million euros followed 200 draws over 67 weeks without a jackpot winner. The 2019 record followed more than a year without a winner. The 2023 record followed almost 21 months without a winner, from May 2021 to February 2023. These are lengths of time, not predictions: a rollover run ends only when a draw produces six matching numbers, and the chance in each draw is the same regardless of how long the run has lasted.

The absence of a cap is a design choice, and it is the reason SuperEnalotto jackpots can exceed those of capped games. It does not make any entry more likely to win during a long run. Lottery outcomes are random. No past result changes the odds of the next draw, and no frequency, hot, cold, or overdue analysis in this record improves the chance of a future result.

title: SuperEnalotto Frequency Method and Simulated-Set Demo
description:
This Signature edition presents an original study of the same subject, written as Signature-original material. Where a point is a design proposal rather than a verified public fact, it is labeled as a Signature design in the text, and it is never presented as an authentic public record.

Frequency analysis for SuperEnalotto counts how often each number from 1 to 90 has appeared in a set of past draws. The method is descriptive: it summarises the past, and in a fair draw it has no bearing on the next result. Because no verified multi-year SuperEnalotto result set was used for this record, the demo runs on a clearly labeled simulated set of draws generated with a fixed seed, and its output must never be presented as real SuperEnalotto history.

The demo generates 300 simulated draws of six numbers each and counts appearances per number. In a fair game the expected count per number is the same for all ninety numbers: 300 draws times 6 numbers divided by 90, which is 20 appearances each on average, with random variation around that average. The simulated counts cluster around 20, which is exactly what a fair random process produces, and any larger spread in a real set would still need a statistical test before it meant anything at all.

Methodology-only note: the demo data is simulated and is not real history. Lottery outcomes are random. No past result changes the odds of the next draw, and no frequency, hot, cold, or overdue analysis in this record improves the chance of a future result.

Labeling note: this Signature record is Signature-original. Verified public facts it repeats are the same facts as in the public edition; any framing, ordering, or extension beyond them is Signature design, not a public record.

demo.code:
import random
random.seed(7)
draws = [sorted(random.sample(range(1, 91), 6)) for _ in range(300)]
counts = {n: 0 for n in range(1, 91)}
for d in draws:
    for n in d:
        counts[n] += 1
print("SIMULATED draws:", len(draws), "(fixed seed 7, not real history)")
print("expected appearances per number:", 300 * 6 // 90)
print("lowest counts:", sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1])[:5])
print("highest counts:", sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1])[-5:])
print("total number slots:", sum(counts.values()))

title: SuperEnalotto Hot Numbers Method
description:
This Signature edition presents an original study of the same subject, written as Signature-original material. Where a point is a design proposal rather than a verified public fact, it is labeled as a Signature design in the text, and it is never presented as an authentic public record.

A hot number is a number that has appeared more often than average in a chosen recent window of draws. The method is sometimes presented as if hot numbers are more likely to appear again, but that presentation is wrong for a fair lottery: each draw selects six numbers from ninety without regard to past draws, so a number's past frequency does not raise or lower its future chance, which stays at 6 in 90 for appearing in the next draw's six main numbers.

The demo below identifies the hottest numbers in the same labeled simulated set used by the frequency record, so the reader can see the method end to end. The hottest numbers in a simulated set are an artefact of random variation in that set, and they carry no information about the next simulated draw, let alone a real one. A reader who checks the demo by re-running it with a different fixed seed will get a different hot list, which is itself the demonstration that hot lists are unstable.

Methodology-only note: the demo data is simulated with a fixed seed and is not real history. Lottery outcomes are random. No past result changes the odds of the next draw, and no frequency, hot, cold, or overdue analysis in this record improves the chance of a future result.

Labeling note: this Signature record is Signature-original. Verified public facts it repeats are the same facts as in the public edition; any framing, ordering, or extension beyond them is Signature design, not a public record.

random.seed(7)
draws = [sorted(random.sample(range(1, 91), 6)) for _ in range(300)]

    for n in d:

hot = sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1])[-6:]
print("SIMULATED set: 300 draws, fixed seed 7 (not real history)")
print("hottest numbers in this simulated set:", hot)

title: SuperEnalotto Cold and Overdue Method
description:
This Signature edition presents an original study of the same subject, written as Signature-original material. Where a point is a design proposal rather than a verified public fact, it is labeled as a Signature design in the text, and it is never presented as an authentic public record.

A cold number is one that has appeared less often than average in a chosen window, and an overdue number is one that has not appeared for a long run of draws. In SuperEnalotto, with ninety numbers and six drawn per draw, the average gap between appearances of any one number is 15 draws, since each draw covers 6 of 90 numbers. Gaps much longer than 15 draws are normal: in a long run of draws, some numbers will inevitably go 40 or 50 draws without appearing, purely by chance.

The demo measures gaps in the same labeled simulated set: for each number, how many simulated draws have passed since its last appearance. The longest gaps in the simulated set are in the range that random variation produces, and they do not make those numbers more likely to appear next. The gambler's error is to treat a long gap as a debt the draw must repay; a fair draw keeps no ledger.

Methodology-only note: the demo data is simulated with a fixed seed and is not real history. Lottery outcomes are random. No past result changes the odds of the next draw, and no frequency, hot, cold, or overdue analysis in this record improves the chance of a future result.

The main-game prize fund is a share of sales, and the jackpot is shared when several lines match, so the expected value of a line depends on the jackpot size and on how many other lines are played, and it is below the 1-euro price in ordinary circumstances.

title: SuperEnalotto Number-Pool Structure Deep Dive: Why Six from Ninety Is So Long
description:
This Signature edition presents an original study of the same subject, written as Signature-original material. Where a point is a design proposal rather than a verified public fact, it is labeled as a Signature design in the text, and it is never presented as an authentic public record.

The jackpot odds grow very fast as the pool grows, because combinations multiply. Choosing six from fifty gives 15,890,700 combinations. Choosing six from sixty gives 50,063,860. Choosing six from seventy gives 131,115,985. Choosing six from eighty gives 300,500,200. Choosing six from ninety gives 622,614,630. Each step of ten in the pool roughly doubles the count, and the jump from eighty to ninety alone adds more than 322 million combinations.

That is why SuperEnalotto's odds are longer than those of EuroMillions, which draws five from fifty plus two stars, and longer than those of Powerball and Mega Millions, which draw five from sixty-nine or seventy plus a bonus ball. The pool is simply larger, and the number of combinations is the whole explanation; no other feature of the game lengthens the odds. The same counting explains why the lower tiers are also longer than in smaller-pool games, and why the two-number tier, at about 1 in 22, is the only tier a regular player meets with any frequency.

Understanding the pool also corrects a common error: adding a second line does not halve the odds in any useful sense. It doubles a very small chance, leaving a very small chance. title: Fallacies Specific to SuperEnalotto
description:
This Signature edition presents an original study of the same subject, written as Signature-original material. Where a point is a design proposal rather than a verified public fact, it is labeled as a Signature design in the text, and it is never presented as an authentic public record.

Several fallacies are specific to the 6-from-90 structure. The first is the belief that the longest odds make the game due to pay out, or that a long rollover run makes the next draw more likely to produce a winner. The chance per draw is always 1 in 622,614,630 per line, and the jackpot grows because nobody has matched, not because a match is becoming more likely. The second is the belief that avoiding birthdays or patterns improves the chance of winning. It changes nothing about matching; it changes only how a prize would be shared if the combination won, because popular combinations are held by more people.

The third fallacy is treating hot, cold, or overdue lists as selections with better odds. The demo records show that hot lists change with the seed and that long gaps are normal in a ninety-number pool. The fourth is the belief that a system entry, which covers many combinations, beats the odds per euro. A system entry buys many chances at the same per-line odds, and its cost rises in proportion to its coverage. The fifth is reading the SuperStar multiplier as an odds improvement: SuperStar changes what a win pays, not how likely the main match is.

All five share one correction: in a fair draw, every combination has the same chance in every draw. Lottery outcomes are random. No past result changes the odds of the next draw, and no frequency, hot, cold, or overdue analysis in this record improves the chance of a future result.

EuroMillions draws five numbers from fifty plus two stars from twelve, and Eurojackpot draws five from fifty plus two from twelve in its current format, while SuperEnalotto draws six from ninety with no separate star pool. The comparison is therefore about pool size and structure: SuperEnalotto's single pool of ninety produces 622,614,630 combinations, far more than either game's main-pool combinations, and that is why its jackpot odds are the longest of the three.

EuroMillions and Eurojackpot cap or roll down their jackpots under their rules, while SuperEnalotto has no cap and no rolldown, so its jackpots can grow for years and reach the record levels listed in this database. EuroMillions and Eurojackpot also pay a second tier through their star matches, while SuperEnalotto pays its second tier through the Jolly, a seventh number drawn from the same pool rather than a separate pool.
